fact_label: CJNG's Mendoza Gaytan ("El Sapo") named national second-in-command, not merely a city plaza boss
value_raw: Hugo Gonzalo Mendoza Gaytan ("El Sapo") named by US authorities as CJNG's national second-in-command (tied with since-captured Audias Flores Silva, "El Jardinero") under new top boss Juan Carlos Valencia Gonzalez ("El Pelon"/"El 03"), following El Mencho's Feb 2026 death -- a materially bigger claim than a single city's plaza boss. Separately, he has led CJNG's "Los Deltas"/"Los Michoacanos" armed cell covering the Jalisco/Nayarit coast (Puerto Vallarta, Nuevo Vallarta, Bahia de Banderas, Sierra Occidente, Valle de Jalisco) since 2017 -- Feb 2026 reporting (pre-dating the national-rank news) named him CJNG's Puerto Vallarta-specific regional chief. Carries a $15 million US reward (DOJ/State Dept, announced 2026-08-05) and is reported -- per Mexico News Daily citing US court filings, not independently primary-source-verified -- to be a godson of El Mencho.

All four consulate PDFs that name income types at all (Houston, Orlando, San Diego, Las Vegas) explicitly and consistently list 'empleo o pensión'/'employment or pension' as the route's two named qualifying income sources under the income leg -- pension proof specified as an original Seguro Social (Mexican Social Security) or foreign pension-institution letter plus 6 months of bank statements showing the deposits; Las Vegas's 2026 PDF additionally names 'an OFFICIAL DOCUMENT THAT STATES RETIREMENT' as an acceptable alternative. The strongest, most uniform finding of this whole extraction pass -- zero consulate-to-consulate divergence found on this dimension.

fact_label: Temporary Resident Visa income-type requirement (ordinary passive)
notes: REAL CONFIRMED CONSULATE-TO-CONSULATE DIVERGENCE, named rather than flattened -- the value above reflects Las Vegas's 2026 PDF only, the single consulate of five checked whose documented list names ordinary passive income at all: under its 'self-employed WITHOUT a registered trade or business' income-proof list it explicitly accepts a 'rental agreement (if income is from rental property)' alongside 1099s/pay stubs/direct-deposit proof. Houston (2025), Orlando, and San Diego (2023) all give a narrower, textually parallel 'empleo o pensión'/'employment or pension' framing for the income leg with no passive/investment/dividend/rental category named anywhere in their document lists -- genuine silence on this dimension at three of four consulates that spell out income types at all, not an explicit rejection, but also not the same open door Las Vegas documents. Chicago's 2023 PDF is generic ('comprobante de ingresos constantes,' proof of constant income) and doesn't resolve the question either way. Read plainly: an applicant with only ordinary passive/investment/dividend income cannot assume every consulate will accept it under the income leg the way Las Vegas's own text does -- the savings/investment balance alternative (already documented, type-independent) is the reliably safe route for that income type everywhere, while the income leg itself is consulate-dependent for this one dimension specifically. Confidence held at Medium, not High, precisely because this is single-consulate primary evidence for an accepted reading, not a cross-corroborated one -- the majority-pattern reading (silent-to-excluded) is real too and is named in full in visa-legal.md, not just in this row's own notes.

World's most congested city in this index; drivers lose an estimated 184 hours/year (~7.6 days) to traffic; 3rd-busiest city in the Americas behind Lima and Toronto. A 3.6% improvement vs. 2024's figure — real but marginal. Walkable colonias (Roma Norte, Condesa) meaningfully soften this if daily life stays concentrated there; crossing the city remains genuinely congested

fact_label: Internet speed - SpeedGEO Mexico City broadband average
notes: Added 2026-08-22 ([specialist]), closing the zero-fact infrastructure-connectivity gap flagged in coverage-summary-2026-08-22 (all five MX locations had zero facts under this criterion). SpeedGEO's dedicated Mexico City page (retrieved via live search this pass, direct fetch 403'd - same access pattern already documented for Oaxaca's testmy.net page in sources.md) reports 37ms average latency; mobile internet separately at 45.2 Mbps down / 13.1 Mbps up; fastest fixed provider Totalplay averaging 178.2 Mbps down over the same window, fastest mobile provider Telcel at 90.7 Mbps down. This is a fresher, directly-sourced, more precise figure than the existing citywide '92.89 Mbps (2026)' line already in overview.md, which carried no source URL - doesn't contradict it, supersedes it as the better-cited number. Consistent with the existing 100-200 Mbps neighborhood-specific figures already documented for Roma Norte/Condesa/Polanco/Coyoacan (this is the citywide aggregate behind those); the existing Cetram-CDMX variance caveat (well-connected colonia vs. 20 minutes away on 10 Mbps cable) still stands and isn't contradicted by this citywide average.

fact_label: Internet speed - SpeedGEO Merida citywide average
notes: Extracted 2026-08-22 ([specialist]) from existing overview.md prose (added 2026-07-19 in the original Merida internet research pass) - closing the zero-fact infrastructure-connectivity gap flagged in coverage-summary-2026-08-22. Totalplay specifically averaged 90.8 Mbps download over the Oct 2024-Sept 2025 window, fastest provider in the city; most home plans run 100-200 Mbps, with 300-500 Mbps common for power users and up to 1,000 Mbps available from Telmex, Totalplay, and Megacable in the best-served areas. Real geographic variance: central/northern Merida (dense, affluent neighborhoods) get genuine fiber-to-the-home competition among multiple ISPs; outlying areas may only have DSL or fixed-wireless, 'often much lower (tens of Mbps)' (multiple ISP-directory sources, 2026). One first-hand digital-nomad account (psimonmyway.com) reports a downtown speed-test result of 242 Mbps down / 206 Mbps up - a genuine data point, not just an aggregate, cited separately in overview.md.

fact_label: Airport access - recurring CNTE teacher-union blockades of Oaxaca International Airport
value_raw: Third confirmed blockade of Xoxocotlan/Oaxaca International Airport (OAX) by CNTE Section 22 as of June 4, 2026 - full terminal-access closure ~9:20am-7:00pm (~10 hours), forcing passengers to walk with luggage to reach flights
notes: No dedicated SpeedGEO/Ookla page exists for Oaxaca City internet speeds (a real, named gap since 2026-07-19, re-checked and still true this pass - testmy.net's Oaxaca City page still 403s on direct fetch) - rather than force a thin/guessed internet-speed fact, this pass researched a different, genuinely load-bearing infrastructure-connectivity finding for Oaxaca: recurring CNTE (teachers' union) road/airport blockades. Corroborated across multiple outlets covering the same May-June 2026 CNTE indefinite work-stoppage wave: UnoTV (https://www.unotv.com/estados/oaxaca/amenaza-cnte-bloqueos-carreteras-accesos-aeropuerto-oaxaca-27-mayo-2026/, threatened May 27), El Financiero and El Sol de Mexico (both reporting the June 3 blockade of the airport plus Pemex terminal and Federal Highway 190), and NMas (10-hour blockade specifically). This is a structurally different and arguably more decision-relevant infrastructure-connectivity fact than a raw Mbps number for a location this remote from a real emergency-care/travel-access reader's perspective: the airport, the region's only realistic fast way in or out, has a documented, recurring (3x in this wave alone), non-hypothetical closure risk tied to Oaxaca's chronic CNTE labor-conflict pattern (see red-flags.md for the broader political/institutional context this sits alongside). Demands centered on repeal of the 2007 ISSSTE law and salary increases - a long-running, cyclical conflict, not a one-off event, which is why this is flagged 'worsening' rather than a settled/stable pattern: blockades recurred three times within roughly one month in this wave alone.
